title.en: Kua Fu Chases the Sun; Xingtian Dances with Shield and Axe

source.work: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), original Chinese text (Guo Pu recension): Kua Fu in 'Haiwai Bei Jing', Xingtian in 'Haixi Jing'

summary.en: Two defiant figures of the Shanhaijing: Kua Fu races the sun, drinks the rivers dry, and dies of thirst, his staff becoming a peach grove; and the headless Xingtian, slain by the Yellow Emperor, makes his nipples his eyes and navel a mouth, dancing forever with shield and battle-axe.
summary.zh: 《山海經》兩位抗爭者：夸父與日逐走，飲盡河渭，道渴而死，棄杖化為鄧林；刑天與帝爭神，帝斷其首，乃以乳為目、以臍為口，操干戚而舞，永不止息。

sensitivity.note: Mythic corpus entry based on classical Chinese sources without a public-domain English translation; passages are condensed paraphrases referenced to modern scholarship. Living cultural heritage of China. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Kua Fu raced with the sun. As he followed it toward Yu Valley, he drank the Yellow River and the Wei River dry; when he turned north to seek the waters of the Great Marsh, he died of thirst on the way. The staff he carried fell to the ground and grew into a peach grove, and the wind and rain feed it still.

[Condensed paraphrase] Xingtian fought the Yellow Emperor for divine supremacy; the Emperor cut off his head and buried it on Changyang Mountain. Headless, Xingtian made his nipples his eyes and his navel a mouth, and he dances still, wielding his shield and battle-axe.

source.archive: Wikisource (reference; Kojiki, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain)
source.work: Kojiki, sections XVIII-XIX: The Eight-Forked Serpent and the Palace of Suga (trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain)

summary.en: Exiled for his ravages, His-Impetuous-Male-Augustness comes to Izumo where the eight-forked serpent of Koshi has devoured seven daughters of an aged couple; he brews eight-fold strong sake, and when the serpent dips each head into a vat and lies drunk, he cuts it apart, finding the sword Kusanagi in its tail.
summary.zh: 暴虐之神須佐之男被逐出高天原，至出雲，遇高志之八岐大蛇——蛇已吞食老夫婦七女。乃釀八醞之酒置於八槽；大蛇垂八首入槽而醉，須佐之男拔劍斬之，於蛇尾中得草薙劍，並娶倖存之櫛名田比賣為妻。

sensitivity.note: Ancient court myth of Japan (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of Chamberlain's public-domain translation. Presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] His-Impetuous-Male-Augustness, expelled from the Plain of High Heaven, came to the upper reaches of the River Hi in Izumo, and found an old man and an old woman weeping, with a young girl between them. They told him the eight-forked serpent of Koshi, with a body spanning eight valleys and eight hills, its eyes like winter cherries, had each year devoured one of their daughters, until only Kushinada-hime remained.

[Condensed paraphrase] Susanoo bade them brew strong sake of eight-fold brewings, and set it in eight vats. The serpent came, dipping a head into each vat, and drank until it was drunk; then Susanoo, drawing the sword ten-grasps long, cut the serpent apart till the blood flowed out — and in the middle of its tail he found a great sword, which he presented to the Sun Goddess, named the Herb-Quelling-Blade of the Great Deity.

title.en: The First Sunrise of the Popol Vuh

region.zh: 瓜地馬拉奇奇卡斯德南哥

texts.period: Popol Vuh, c. 1554-58 (copy of older traditions)

source.work: H. H. Bancroft, The Native Races of the Pacific States, vol. III: Myths and Languages (1875), Quiche chapter retelling the Popol Vuh

summary.en: Before the dawn of the present sun, the first men of wood were destroyed; the true people — made of yellow and white maize dough — gathered at the place of raising their faces to await the first light. The morning star came forth, and the sun shown like a white flash of lightning, drying the face of the earth, as the ancestors sang the raising of the heart of the sky.
summary.zh: 太陽未昇之世，木人已滅；真民——黃白玉米所塑——齊聚「仰面之地」以待初光。晨星先出，太陽如白電乍現，烘乾大地之面；先祖遂歌詠天心之高舉。

sensitivity.note: K'iche' Maya mythic corpus (Popol Vuh); passages are condensed paraphrases of the council-book's narrative. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When the true people had been fashioned from yellow and white maize by the Creator and the Maker, they could see to the ends of the earth, and they gave thanks on the surface of the earth; but the gods dimmed their eyes as a man dims a mirror when he breathes on it, so that they might see only what was near.

[Condensed paraphrase] They waited there in the dark, holding the hearts of their hearts, until the great star came forth before the sun, and then the sun itself shown like a white ray of lightning, turning the faces of the carved images of the animals of old to stone, while the true people watched the sun's face rise, and the sky and the earth were glad.

title.en: Sventovit of Arkona and the White Horse
title.zh: 斯文托維特與白馬神諭

region.zh: 波羅的海呂根島阿科納

texts.period: 12th-13th c. Danish/German chronicles (Saxo, Book XIV; Helmold of Bosau)

source.work: Jan Machal, 'Slavic Mythology', in The Mythology of All Races, vol. III (1918), Part II ch. I 'Svantovit'

summary.en: On the cliff of Arkona stood the great temple of Sventovit, god of the Rani, served by a horse kept for the god: each year the priests set the white horse's hoof against three pairs of spears to divine war or peace; victory in battle belonged to whoever took the omens with the horn of mead, and the god's quadruple horn was filled each year with wine.
summary.zh: 阿科納崖上立蘭尼人之大神斯文托維特聖殿；殿中養神馬為占：歲首祭司以神馬之蹄踏三重並置之雙矛，以卜戰和。出征者執蜜酒之角以受吉兆；神之四角蜜酒歲滿則傾而再斟。

sensitivity.note: Pre-Christian Slavic tradition surviving only through Christian chronicles (Saxo, Helmold, the Russian Primary Chronicle); passages are condensed paraphrases of the chroniclers' accounts — reconstruction status should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] On the cliff of Arkona on the isle of Rügen rose the wooden temple of Sventovit, with its one great door and carved inner chamber, hung with purple and crowded with the horns of princes. The god's image held a drinking-horn each year refilled with mead, and a white horse was kept in the enclosure; only the priest might feed and ride it.

[Condensed paraphrase] Before a war the priests set three rows of crossed spears, led the horse over them, and if it stepped first with the right foot the venture was blessed; the horse was also run at dawn through triple spear-lines each year. The people said the god rode his horse at night against their enemies, and his oracle decided war, peace, seed-time and harvest.

title.en: Svarog and Dazhbog, the Heavenly Father and Sun Prince
title.zh: 斯瓦羅格與達日博格：天父與日君

texts.period: Russian Primary Chronicle, year 980 CE entry (later compilations)

source.work: Jan Machal, 'Slavic Mythology', in The Mythology of All Races, vol. III (1918), on Svarog, Dazhbog and Svarozic, and the Deities of the Pagan Russians

summary.en: The chronicle's heathen pantheon of Prince Vladimir lists Dazhbog among the idols of the Kyiv hill; the scholia to an Old Russian translation of John Malalas makes Svarog the heavenly smith-father who reigned in the age of tools, and his son Dazhbog 'the Sun' who reigned after him — giving fire and light to the Rus' people.
summary.zh: 編年史載弗拉基米爾王於基輔山丘所立神像中有達日博格；古俄譯約翰·馬拉拉斯史書之邊注則謂：天匠斯瓦羅格治器物之世，其子「日」達日博格繼之為君——賜火與光於羅斯之民。

sensitivity.note: Pre-Christian Slavic tradition surviving through chronicle references and later scholia; passages are condensed paraphrases — reconstruction status should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] When Prince Vladimir ruled in Kyiv he set idols on the hill: Perun of wood with silver head, and Hors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokosh. The people sacrificed to them, calling their sons and daughters to the hill, and the heathen gods of the old Russians were honored with offerings.

[Condensed paraphrase] In the scholia appended to the Old Russian translation of the Chronicle of John Malalas, the heavenly smith Svarog is said to have reigned in Egypt in the days when tongs and hammers first fell from heaven; and after him his son, called Dazhbog, 'the giving lord,' ruled as the Sun — for the heathen named the Sun the son of Svarog, who gives warmth and light to all the world.

title.en: Jumong, Born of Light and River

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, vol. 1 (1905), Ko-gu-ryu chapter (Chu-mong legend)

summary.en: Habaek's daughter Yuhwa, impregnated by sunlight, lays an egg in leather that a boy of wondrous speech breaks forth from in seven days; pursued by the princes of Buyeo, Jumong warns the river, and fish and turtles rise to bridge the water under him — he crosses, founds Goguryeo, and is the Heavenly King of the East.
summary.zh: 河伯之女柳花感日光而孕，產一卵於革囊；七日卵中出一語奇之童。扶餘王子欲害之，朱蒙告於河：魚鱉浮而為橋，履之而渡——遂東至紇升骨城，建高句麗，是為東明聖王。

sensitivity.note: Foundational myth recorded in Korea's oldest court chronicles; passages are condensed paraphrases of the Samguk Sagi/Yusa narratives. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The daughter of the river god Habaek, called Yuhwa, was carried off by the heavenly king and made pregnant by a ray of sunlight; her father, shamed, shut her in a leather sack and threw it into the river, where it floated to a king's court. The child hatched from an egg, and the king raised the boy, named Jumong, a master bowman.

[Condensed paraphrase] When the princes of Buyeo plotted against him, Jumong fled to the great river and, striking the water with his bow, cried that he was the grandson of Heaven and the River; fish and turtles rose in shoals to make a bridge of their backs. He crossed over the crossing of them, the bridge sank behind, and he came to the hill of Holbon and made his capital, calling his kingdom Goguryeo.

title.en: Suro of Gaya Born from Six Golden Eggs

source.work: Homer B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, vol. 1 (1905), Kingdom of Ka-rak section

summary.en: The six elders of Gujiguk prayed without rest for a king; a voice from heaven promised to send one, and nine chiefs sailed out to find a ship bearing a red banner and a red sail moored on the sand — from six golden eggs came six boys, the firstborn Suro king of Geumgwan Gaya, and the five other kings of the Gaya states.
summary.zh: 龜旨國九干晝夜祈禱求王；天音許之，遣九長老出海尋訪——果見赤帆赤旗之船泊於龜旨峰下沙灘。船中六金卵化為六童，長者首露為金海伽倻之王，餘五卵為五伽倻列國之君。

sensitivity.note: Foundational myth recorded in the Samguk Yusa; passages are condensed paraphrases of the Garak records. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] The chiefs of the nine villages of Gujiguk gathered on the peak of Kui-ji (Turtle Peak) and prayed day and night for a king to rule them; a voice from heaven answered that it would send down a ruler, and told them to wash, pound the earth, and set out wine and food before looking out on the sea.

[Condensed paraphrase] They sailed out and found a ship moored by the sandhill, flying a red banner and red sail; in it were six golden eggs which turned into beautiful boys. The first to be born they named Suro, and he became the king of Geumgwan Gaya; his five brothers became the kings of the other Gaya states, and the queen who came to him, Heo Hwang-ok, arrived likewise from a far land by sea.

title.en: The Kumulipo: Life from the Deep Darkness
title.zh: 庫木里波：幽暗深處的生命

texts.period: Kumulipo chant, committed to writing c. 18th-19th c.; trans. Queen Liliuokalani, 1897

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; Kumulipo, trans. Queen Liliuokalani)
source.work: The Kumulipo, a Hawaiian creation chant, trans. Queen Lili'uokalani (1897)

summary.en: The Kumulipo, the Hawaiian chant of genealogy, opens in the deep darkness of Po: in the first age the coral polyp is born, then the fish of the sea and the creeping things; night and day, dark and light follow one another, generation after generation, until the ages of the gods give way to the ages of men — the chiefly line born from darkness into light.
summary.zh: 庫木里波為夏威夷系譜頌歌：起於暗夜「坡」之深處——第一紀珊瑚蟲出生，繼而海魚、蠕行之物；夜與晝相代，一代復一代，直至神紀讓於人紀——酋長世系自幽暗生於光明。

sensitivity.note: Hawaiian genealogical chant recorded in the 18th-19th century and translated by Queen Lili'uokalani (1897); passages are condensed paraphrases. Living tradition of Hawai'i — presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Native Hawaiian communities.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In the first age of the Kumulipo, born was the coral polyp in the sea, born the worm that creeps, born the shellfish and the swarming things; born in the sea the fish, and on the land the man. Night began, night ended: the deep darkness of Po brought forth, and the light of day followed after.

[Condensed paraphrase] Age followed upon age, the dark with the dark giving birth to the finned and the creeping, until the age was born of the woman and the man; the chant runs down the generations of the gods to the generations of the chiefs, for the child of chiefly blood is born from the deep darkness into the world of light.

title.en: Hina, the Sky-Mother of Hawaiian Chants
title.zh: 希娜：夏威夷頌歌中的天母

texts.period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded 19th c. (Fornander Collection)

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities)
source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-lore: Hina and Māui narratives

summary.en: In the Fornander chants, Hina the mother of Māui dwells in the moon, beating her tapa cloth; her son Māui the demigod snares the sun on Haleakala with ropes plaited by her hands, forcing it to slow its journey so the days might be long enough for men to dry their kapa and cook their food.
summary.zh: 弗南德爾歌集所載：毛伊之母希娜居月中，晝夜擣樹皮布；其子半神毛伊以母所編之繩於哈萊亞卡拉縛日，迫其緩行——庶使白晝延長，民得曝布炊食。

sensitivity.note: Hawaiian oral tradition recorded in the 19th century; passages are condensed paraphrases of the Fornander Collection narratives. Living tradition of Hawai'i — presented as an archival record, not as permission to speak for Native Hawaiian communities.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Hina, the woman of the moon, beat her kapa cloth under the full moon's light, and her strokes were the thunder; her sons were the small Māui of many wonders, who fished islands from the sea with the hook manaiakalani, the fishhook of the great land.

[Condensed paraphrase] Because the days were too short for the work of men, Māui took the ropes his mother had plaited, climbed to the crater of the great mountain, and laid snares upon the sun's rays as they broke over the rim; the sun cried out and promised to travel slowly across the sky forever — and thus the days grew long for all the people.

source.work: Lewis Spence, Myths & Legends of Babylonia & Assyria (1916), 'The Descent of Ishtar into Hades'

summary.en: The goddess Inanna abandons her temples to descend to the netherworld and seize the seat of her sister Ereshkigal; stripped of one power at each of seven gates, she stands naked before the throne and is struck dead — until wise Enki creates two sexless beings who win her corpse and revive her with the food and water of life, and galla demons demand she give a substitute to go free.
summary.zh: 女神伊南娜棄其七廟而降冥府，欲奪姊埃雷什基伽勒之位；過七門，一門除一力，至御前裸然而立，遂遭誅——智神恩基造二無性之人，媚於冥后而得屍，以生命之食水活之；冥界群魔隨之索替死者。

sensitivity.note: Sumerian mythic text; passages are condensed paraphrases referenced to the ETCSL scholarly translation. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] From the great heaven she set her mind on the great below: the holy priestess Inanna abandoned her temples of heaven and earth and went down to the netherworld. At each of the seven gates of the land of no return, the keeper removed from her a garment of her power, until she stood naked before Ereshkigal on the throne, and the judges of the underworld fixed on her the eye of death.

[Condensed paraphrase] Her minister Ninshubur pleaded at the temples until Enki, the god of wisdom, made from the dirt of his nails two sexless creatures who slipped into the underworld, sympathized with the mourning queen, and won the corpse; they sprinkled it with the food and water of life, and Inanna rose. But the galla demons rose at her side, and she went from city to city mourning, until she found her husband Dumuzi on his throne and set the demons upon him.

title.en: The Wayang Cycle: Rama in Java

texts.period: Old Javanese Ramayana (kakawin, c. 9th c. CE) and wayang tradition

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), chs. XII-XIV (Hindu Javanese literature; the wayang)

summary.en: The Indian epic arrived early in Java, where the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin retold Rama's war against the giant-king Rawana, and the wayang shadow theatre made Rama, his monkey ally Hanuman, and the ten-faced Rawana the fixed figures of a nightly shadow-myth that Javanese courts have treated as sacred genealogy.
summary.zh: 印度史詩早傳爪哇：古爪哇《羅摩衍那》頌詩重述羅摩征討十面巨靈王拉瓦納之戰；哇揚皮影戲遂以羅摩、神猴哈奴曼與十首拉瓦納為夜夜搬演之定角，爪哇歷朝視為神聖譜系。

sensitivity.note: Javanese adaptation of the Ramayana tradition; passages are condensed paraphrases referencing the kakawin and wayang scholarship. Presented as a comparative-mythology text. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Rama of Ayodhya, exiled with his wife Sinta, lost her to the giant-king Rawana of Alengka, who carried her over the sea to his island city; with the monkey general Hanuman and the army of the monkeys, Rama built a bridge across the water, burned the city's gate, and killed Rawana and his host to take back his wife.

[Condensed paraphrase] The court poets of Java rendered the war in the kakawin, and the dalang (puppet-master) of the wayang kulit performs it by lamplight to this day: the dalang is considered to sanctify the audience as he speaks the gods' parts, and the story is told as both legend and royal genealogy, for Javanese kings claimed descent from Rama's line.

title.en: Sang Sapurba Descends from the Hill of Light
title.zh: 山格山普巴：自光山而下

region.zh: 印尼蘇門答臘巴鄰旁西貢塘山

texts.period: Malay Annals (Sulalat al-Salatin), 17th c. compilation of older legends; trans. Leyden, 1821

source.archive: Internet Archive (reference; The Malay Annals, trans. John Leyden)
source.work: Malay Annals (Sulalat al-Salatin), trans. John Leyden (1821): the descent of Sang Sapurba

summary.en: The Malay Annals open the line of the Malayan kings at the hill of Siguntang-gunung above Palembang, where the divine Raja Sang Sapurba appeared in the age of Pandai-pandai, showing himself to be of the race of the kings of the world; his princely greatness was first shown when he drew the wondrous sword from the river and wed the king's daughter — from his descent the Malay royal lines are traced.
summary.zh: 《馬來紀年》以巴鄰旁上方西貢塘山為馬來諸王之始：神君山格山普巴顯聖於班代時代，示其為世界列王之裔；其「王者之德」初現於拔劍出水、迎娶公主之事——馬來蘇丹世系由此而開。

sensitivity.note: Malay royal myth recorded in the Sulalat al-Salatin; passages are condensed paraphrases of Leyden's 1821 public-domain translation. Presented as a comparative-mythology text.

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] At the foot of the hill of Siguntang-gunung, on the banks of the river of Palembang, the people of the age of Pandai-pandai beheld a prince of divine aspect descend from the hill, washing in the water; the king gave him his daughter, and because he wore the signs of the race of the kings of the world he was called Sang Sapurba, the great prince of descent.

[Condensed paraphrase] When he drew from the river the wonderful sword that appeared on the water's surface, the greatness of his soul was made manifest, and the people took him for their king; the line of the Malay kings of Minangkabau, of Singapore, and of Melaka is traced in the Annals to this descent from the hill of light.

title.en: Dewi Sri and the Rice That Rises from the Body

texts.period: Javanese-Sundanese rice mythology, older than the Hindu period

source.work: J. G. Frazer, The S. of the Corn and of the Wild (The Golden Bough pt. V, vol. I, 1912), East-Indian rice-ceremony section

summary.en: The rice-goddess of Java and Bali: in the Sundanese cycle the heavenly maiden Pohaci Sanghyang Asri, hounded by desire she cannot answer, is buried by the gods — and from her head the coconut springs, from her lips the betel, from her body the rice that feeds the world; her serpent-consort, the god of the field, protects the seed.
summary.zh: 爪哇與巴厘之稻神：巽他神話中天上仙女波哈奇桑揚阿斯里因無法回應之情所困，眾神葬之——頭生椰子，唇生蔞葉，身化稻米以養萬民；其蛇伴田神護種於田。

sensitivity.note: Javanese and Sundanese agricultural myth; passages are condensed paraphrases of the rice-goddess cycles. Living cultural heritage of Indonesia. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Pohaci Sanghyang Asri, the maiden of heaven, was so beautiful that all the gods desired her; because she could not answer their desire without breaking her virtue, the gods in sorrow killed her and buried her body in the earth so that something good might come of her death.

[Condensed paraphrase] From her head grew the coconut-palm, from her lips the betel-vine, from her eyes the many kinds of spice, from her body the rice that gives life to the world; the serpent that guarded the fields became her consort, and the rice goddess Dewi Sri is worshipped still in the planting and harvest of Java and Bali.

title.en: Dievs, Saule, and the Celestial Wedding of the Dainas
title.zh: 笛維斯、紹蕾與達伊納天婚

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（利夫蘭與庫爾蘭）

texts.period: Dainas (Latvian folk songs) collected from the 19th c.

summary.en: The Latvian dainas sing a sky-court of gods: Dievs the Father of the sky, Saule the Sun-mother whose daughters wash her gold in the sea, Meness the Moon who loves the sun's daughter — the celestial wedding of the sun's daughter is the great daina theme, with the bathers, the weavers, and the mourners of the gods below.
summary.zh: 拉脫維亞達伊納短歌唱天上神廷：天父笛維斯、日母紹蕾（其女於海中洗金）、月神梅內斯戀日女——太陽女兒之天婚為達伊納之要題；神之浴者、織者與哭喪者皆在其間。

sensitivity.note: Baltic mythic corpus of the dainas (folk songs with mythic content); passages are condensed paraphrases — reconstruction status of the deity list should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] In the dainas Dievs the sky-father rides in the longest autumn nights to see the green fields, and rings the silver bell; Saule the sun-mother drives her chariot across the hill of the sky, and her daughters wash her golden girdle in the sea at evening.

[Condensed paraphrase] The great wedding of the dainas is the wedding of the sun's daughter: Meness the moon, or Auseklis the morning star, rides to the bridal hill; the guests sit at the table of the celestial stone, and the Latvian singers made of this sky-wedding the image of their own year — light and dark, sowing and harvest.

region.zh: 拉脫維亞（庫爾茲梅與道加瓦河）

texts.period: Latvian national epic (Andrejs Pumpurs, 1888) built on folk myth

source.work: Andrejs Pumpurs, Lacplesis (1888), Latvian original of the national epic

summary.en: The folk layers of the Latvian epic: Lacplesis, born of a bear-woman, slays the monstrous bear that devours the land's herds, wears its ears as his mark, and defends the Latvian shore against the Black Knight — the folk song figures of the bear-son and the hero of the Daugava gathered into a national myth of freedom.
summary.zh: 拉脫維亞史詩之民間層：拉奇普萊西斯為熊母所生，誅食畜之怪熊，以其耳為記；守道加瓦河岸而抗黑騎士——民間歌謠中熊子與河上英雄之形象，匯為民族自由之神話。

sensitivity.note: Latvian epic built on folk mythic material; passages are condensed paraphrases — the epic is a 19th-century literary construction on folk songs and its content is treated as mythic corpus. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Lacplesis was the son of a bear and a human mother, and grew in the forests of Kurzeme, strong beyond all men; when the monstrous bear laid waste the herds of the people, he fought it in its den and strangled it, wearing its torn ears upon his head — hence his name, the Bear-Slayer.

[Condensed paraphrase] By the Daugava he met the Black Knight who ruled the river with fire and iron; in the folk layers the hero was promised to the land until the day he should be cast into the river by the Black Knight — and the singers said the Latvian nation would rise when Lacplesis should wake again from the river's bed.

title.en: Jurate and Kastytis: The Amber Palace of the Sea
title.zh: 尤拉特與卡斯蒂蒂斯：海上琥珀宮

region.zh: 立陶宛波羅的海海岸（帕蘭加）

texts.period: Lithuanian folk legend recorded from the 19th c.

source.work: Ludwik Adam Jucewicz, Wspomnienia Zmudzi (1842), 'Krolowa morza Baltyckiego' (Queen of the Baltic Sea)

summary.en: Jurate, the goddess who ruled the Baltic sea from an amber palace, took pity on the fisherman Kastytis whose nets the waves tore, and loved him; Perkunas, the thunder-god, wrecked the amber palace with a lightning bolt for her betrayal of the sea — and the pieces of the palace still wash up as amber on the shore of Palanga.
summary.zh: 海上女神尤拉特居琥珀宮而統波羅的海；憫漁人卡斯蒂蒂斯網破之苦而相愛。雷神佩爾庫納斯怒其背海之約，以雷火轟碎琥珀宮——帕蘭加海岸至今猶拾宮殿之碎屑，是為琥珀。

sensitivity.note: Lithuanian folk legend; passages are condensed paraphrases — reconstruction status of Baltic myth should be treated with care. [Citation provenance: the original Wikipedia reference was replaced with the verified public-domain source recorded here.]

passages.text: [Condensed paraphrase] Jurate the sea-maiden ruled the deep in a palace built of amber under the Baltic waves; when the fisherman Kastytis dared to fish in her waters and his nets were cut by her servants, she rose in anger to chide him — and finding him fair, took him to the amber palace and loved him.

[Condensed paraphrase] Perkunas the thunder-god, keeper of order among the gods, came in fury at the goddess's love for a mortal; his lightning broke the amber palace and struck Kastytis dead in its ruins. The sea keeps Jurate bound to the wreck, and the fishermen of Palanga gather the little pieces of the palace that the waves still cast up, which men call amber.
